subtitle: Design the routines that let a division learn from its own work: how bad news reaches leaders, how reviews happen after something goes wrong and how people closest to the community shape decisions before they are final.
audience: For managers, directors and senior leaders in DHS and DSD. It supports leadership practice; personnel actions, formal investigations and policy approvals follow the agency's established processes.

lessons.title: Culture is built by systems
objectives: Describe a learning organization as one that notices what is not working and changes before a crisis.
Explain how leaders teach culture through what they pay attention to and how they react to problems.
Recognize how concentrated decision-making also concentrates information.
Treat resistance to a change as information about the change.
lessons.teaching:
A learning organization notices what is not working and changes without waiting for a crisis. David Garvin, Amy Edmondson and Francesca Gino describe three building blocks: a supportive learning environment, where people feel safe to disagree and admit mistakes; concrete learning processes, such as experiments and reviews; and leadership that reinforces learning. All three depend on routines more than on smart individuals.

Edgar Schein's work on culture shows that leaders teach culture through what they pay attention to, how they react to critical incidents and what they reward. Those signals outweigh any values statement. A director who asks "what are we missing?" teaches something different from one who asks "who approved this?"

Power and information travel together. When decisions sit with a few people, staff stop sharing what those people cannot or will not act on, and leaders decide with half the picture. Tema Okun's list of organizational habits names power hoarding, treating the written word as the only valid evidence and either/or thinking among the patterns that can narrow what leaders hear. What a case manager hears at a kitchen table, or what a county partner sees in a waiting room, is evidence too.

Either/or thinking hides options. "Either we enforce the new process or we make exceptions" leaves out the third choice: learn why the process is not working and fix it.
lessons.keyPoint: Leaders teach culture through what they pay attention to and how they react to problems. Those signals outweigh any values statement.
lessons.example: Practice case: Three months after a new intake process launched, a manager in the leadership meeting says frontline staff are "resisting" it. The director has heard the same from two other supervisors.
lessons.question: What should the director say?
choices: "What are they seeing that we aren't?"
feedback: It restates the rule and misses the chance to learn why staff are struggling.
This treats resistance as information and opens a path to fix the process.
Patience can help, and without a question attached it can also delay a needed fix.
lessons.reflection: What does your division pay attention to most in leadership meetings? What might staff conclude from that?
lessons.action: List the last three topics that took the most time in your leadership meetings. Write one sentence on what each one signals to staff about what matters.

check.question: Which is one of the three building blocks of a learning organization described by Garvin, Edmondson and Gino?
wrong: A detailed policy manual for every situation.
Hiring only the most experienced staff.
check.feedback: The three building blocks are a supportive learning environment, concrete learning processes and leadership that reinforces learning. Manuals and experience help, but they do not make an organization learn.

lessons.title: How bad news travels
objectives: Map how a problem on the front line reaches a leader.
Count the places where a message can soften, stall or stop.
Respond to bad news in a way that makes people willing to bring it again.
Build at least one direct channel from frontline staff and partners.
lessons.teaching:
Draw how a problem on the front line reaches you. A case manager notices something, tells a supervisor, who mentions it to a manager, who includes it in a monthly report, which a director reads. Count the steps. Each one is a place where the message can soften, stall or stop. Many leaders find that the news arrives months late, if at all.

Your first reaction to bad news is a signal. The first time someone brings you a problem, how you respond tells them whether to do it again, and tells everyone they talk to. Thank them before you respond to the content. Ask one question. Decide what you will do and tell them.

Direct channels shorten the path. A quarterly listening session with frontline staff, a standing agenda item for partner concerns or a simple rule that every new process gets a 60-day check with the people using it. These routines bring information forward on a schedule rather than waiting for a complaint.

A learning organization still makes decisions and holds people accountable. It learns before it blames. A division learns at the speed its leaders can hear bad news.
lessons.keyPoint: A division learns at the speed its leaders can hear bad news. Thank the messenger before you respond to the message.
lessons.example: Practice case: The case manager asks for five minutes with the director and explains that the new intake form is causing families to give up partway through. The director championed the form.
lessons.question: What is the director's best first response?
choices: Explain why the form was designed the way it was.
Thank the case manager, ask where families are stopping and say when the director will follow up.
Tell the case manager to raise it through their supervisor.
feedback: The explanation may be accurate, and it signals that bad news is met with a defense.
Thanks first, a question second and a clear follow-up make it more likely that the case manager, and others, bring problems forward again.
The chain of command has value, and redirecting this moment teaches people that going direct is not welcome.
lessons.reflection: What is something your division knows that you, as a leader, may not? How would it reach you?
lessons.action: Draw the path a frontline problem takes to reach you. Count the steps and choose one to shorten.

check.question: Why does a leader's first reaction to bad news matter so much?
check.correct: It tells the person, and others who hear about it, whether bringing problems forward is worth the risk.
wrong: It determines whether the leader is legally responsible.
It is the only chance to correct the person who made the mistake.
check.feedback: People watch how leaders react. A defensive or blaming response teaches the division to stay quiet, and the next problem arrives later.

lessons.title: Blameless reviews
objectives: Run a review that asks what happened and what the system made easy or hard, without assigning blame.
Set ground rules aloud and hold them when someone starts to blame.
Invite the people who did the work, including partners.
End a review with a small number of changes, each with an owner.
lessons.teaching:
After something goes wrong, a blameless review asks what happened, what made sense to people at the time and what the system made easy or hard. It leaves out who to blame. People tell the truth when it is safe to, and the truth is what you need to fix the system.

Amy Edmondson's research describes a spectrum of reasons for failure, from deliberate rule-breaking to complexity and thoughtful experiments. Most failures in complex work come from the process, not from deliberate choices. Treating them as blameworthy teaches people to hide them. A blameless review does not excuse deliberate misconduct. That goes through the agency's formal processes, separately.

Running a review well takes a few habits. Invite the people who did the work, including partners who saw the effects. Say the ground rules aloud at the start. Use a facilitator who did not make the decision. When someone starts to name a person, redirect gently to the process. End with two or three changes and an owner and date for each.

Forty-five minutes is often enough. The goal is not a perfect report. It is a few changes that make the next time better, and a team that is willing to come to the next review.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask what happened, what made sense at the time and what the system made easy or hard. End with a few changes, each with an owner.
lessons.example: Practice case: In a blameless review of a missed deadline, the supervisor starts to say which case manager made the error. The facilitator, who did not make the decision under review, is leading the session.
lessons.question: What should the facilitator do?
choices: Gently redirect: "Let's stay with what the process made easy or hard."
feedback: The room learns that this review is about blame after all, and people will say less.
This keeps the ground rules and keeps people willing to speak. The individual concern, if any, can be handled separately.
It avoids conflict and loses the learning.
lessons.reflection: Think of a decision in your division that did not work out. What would a blameless review have found that a search for fault did not?
lessons.action: Choose one recent decision that went wrong. Plan a 45-minute blameless review: who to invite, the ground rules you will say aloud and who will facilitate.

check.question: What does a blameless review leave out?
check.correct: Assigning blame to individuals for what went wrong.
check.feedback: A blameless review looks closely at what happened and ends with changes. It leaves blame out so people can speak honestly. Deliberate misconduct is handled through separate formal processes.

lessons.title: Sharing decisions before they are final
objectives: Bring a draft decision to the people it affects before it is final.
Ask focused questions that make review quick and useful.
Distinguish sharing before deciding from needing consensus.
Build feedback loops that continue after a decision is made.
lessons.teaching:
Bring a draft to the people it affects and ask what you missed. You keep the decision. You lose the surprises. Feedback after a decision is final rarely changes it, and partners and staff know that, so they often stop offering it.

Make review quick and focused. One week, two or three specific questions and a clear statement of what can still change. "Does this notice make sense to a family reading it for the first time? What would make the new timeline hard for counties?" gets better answers than "Any feedback?"

Sharing before deciding is not the same as needing agreement. Some decisions are urgent, and some are constrained by law or budget. Say so. People can accept a decision they disagree with when they were heard and understand the reasons.

Feedback loops that last outlive any single decision. A 60-day check on every new process, a standing agenda item for partner concerns and a short report back on what changed because of feedback. Reporting back is the step most often skipped, and it is the one that tells people their input mattered.
lessons.keyPoint: Share the draft before it is final. You keep the decision. You lose the surprises.
lessons.example: Practice case: The program manager has a draft policy ready to send. The county partner and the counties they represent have not seen it. The policy changes how families submit paperwork.
lessons.question: What should the program manager do?
choices: Send it and invite feedback afterward.
Share the draft with the county partner's group for one week, with two focused questions.
Hold it until every partner agrees.
feedback: Feedback after a decision is final rarely changes it, and partners know that.
A short, focused review catches problems early and builds trust, without giving up the decision.
Consensus can stall urgent work. Sharing before deciding is not the same as needing agreement.
lessons.reflection: When were you last surprised by the effects of a decision you made? Who could have told you in advance?
lessons.action: Pick one decision you will make in the next month. Name the people it affects and write two questions to ask them before it is final.

check.question: What is the main purpose of sharing a draft decision before it is final?
check.correct: To catch problems and effects the decision-maker cannot see, while there is still time to change the decision.
wrong: To get everyone's agreement before acting.
To share responsibility if the decision goes wrong.
check.feedback: Sharing early improves the decision. The leader still decides, and does not need consensus or someone to share blame.

cards.back: An organization that notices what is not working and changes before a crisis, through routines rather than individual heroics.
A supportive learning environment, concrete learning processes and leadership that reinforces learning.
A drawing of how a frontline problem reaches a leader. Each step is a place the message can soften, stall or stop.
Asks what happened, what made sense at the time and what the system made easy or hard. Ends with a few changes and owners.
Bring the draft to the people it affects. You keep the decision. You lose the surprises.
Tell people what changed because of their input. The step most often skipped.

aid.heading: Hear bad news well
items: Say what you will do and when.

aid.heading: Run a blameless review
items: Invite the people who did the work, including partners.
Use a facilitator who did not make the decision.
End with two or three changes, each with an owner and date.

aid.heading: Share a decision before it is final
items: Give a short window, such as one week.
Ask two or three focused questions.
Say what can still change and what cannot.

aid.heading: Feedback loops that last
items: A 60-day check on every new process.
A quarterly listening session with frontline staff.
A standing agenda item for partner concerns.

sources.title: David A. Garvin, Amy C. Edmondson and Francesca Gino — Is Yours a Learning Organization?, Harvard Business Review (2008)
sources.note: Describes three building blocks of a learning organization: a supportive learning environment, concrete learning processes and leadership that reinforces learning.

sources.title: Amy C. Edmondson — Strategies for Learning from Failure, Harvard Business Review (2011)
sources.note: Describes a spectrum of reasons for failure and how treating most failures as blameworthy leads people to hide them.

sources.title: Amy Edmondson — Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
sources.note: The 1999 Administrative Science Quarterly article, hosted by MIT. Supports the link between psychological safety and team learning behavior.

sources.title: Edgar H. Schein — Organizational Culture, American Psychologist (1990)
sources.note: Describes how culture is learned and how leaders shape it, including through what they pay attention to and how they react to critical incidents.

sources.title: Tema Okun, White Supremacy Culture: Characteristics (updated 2025)
sources.note: Source for power hoarding, worship of the written word and either/or thinking as organizational habits. Okun describes the list as a tool for reflection and cautions against using it to accuse people; it is not an empirical diagnostic instrument.
